deed: ג׳ושוע לדרברג מגלה שחיידקים מחליפים גנים וזוכה בפרס נובל בגיל 33
title: Joshua Lederberg discovered that bacteria exchange genes, and won the Nobel Prize at 33

trailer.text: For a long time it was thought that bacteria multiply by dividing, and that all bacteria therefore have the same genetic make-up.
In 1946, Lederberg and Edward Tatum showed that bacteria's genes can also change in a way similar to sexual reproduction.
Two bacteria can exchange genetic material with one another and pass pieces of DNA across a bridge-like connection.
Lederberg was 33 when he won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery, and was one of the youngest laureates.

paragraphs.text: For a long time it was thought that bacteria multiply by dividing, and that all bacteria therefore have the same genetic make-up.
According to the Times, scientists at the time believed that bacteria reproduced asexually, by dividing into genetically identical halves.
According to Rockefeller, through the 1940s the accepted view was that bacteria do not have genetic mechanisms similar to those of higher organisms.
Scientists knew that some bacteria cause life-threatening diseases.
They also knew that some are resistant even to the strongest antibiotics.
In 1944, Avery, McCarty and MacLeod discovered that DNA is the genetic material in Pneumococcus.
The discovery was not connected to a method of reproduction, and was met with widespread skepticism.

stations.title: A rabbi's son who chose science

paragraphs.text: Lederberg was born on May 23, 1925, in Montclair, New Jersey.
His father was an Orthodox rabbi, and his mother came from a family that included Torah scholars.
According to the National Library of Medicine, despite his biblical name, Lederberg was drawn to science at an early age.
According to Stanford, as a teenager he promised to help humanity through science rather than through faith.
In 1943 he joined a Navy medical training program.
He worked at a naval hospital, examining soldiers for malaria parasites.
Inspired by the new evidence about DNA, Lederberg interrupted medical school to pursue experimental genetics with Edward Tatum of Yale.
According to the Nobel Prize website, after studying medicine at Columbia from 1944 to 1946, Lederberg moved to Yale to work with Edward Tatum.
According to the National Library of Medicine, after initial failures Lederberg proposed to Tatum that they work together.
In 1946, during a year-long leave from medical school, he carried out experiments with the intestinal bacterium E. coli.
In the first experiments he estimated that only one in every 20 strains is fertile.

He crossed two strains of E. coli, each with a different mutation that caused a nutritional deficiency, and found that some of the offspring again produced the substances their parents could not produce.
Some of the offspring again produced the substances that their parents could not produce.
In this way Lederberg and Tatum showed that bacteria's genes can also change in a way similar to sexual reproduction.
Two bacteria join through a bridge-like connection and pass pieces of DNA through it.
Lederberg named the process "conjugation," received his doctorate for the research and officially left medical school.
According to his autobiography on the Nobel Prize website, in 1947 Lederberg was appointed assistant professor of genetics at the University of Wisconsin, and his Yale doctorate was awarded in 1948.
In 1947 Lederberg left Yale for the University of Wisconsin, where he continued to study bacterial genetics.
He developed a technique for identifying strains resistant to antibiotics or to bacteriophage without exposing them to these.
In this way he proved that resistance is a genetic mutation rather than an adaptation.
At Wisconsin he helped prove that genetic mutations occur spontaneously.
According to Rockefeller, with the student Norton Zinder he showed that bacteriophages can transfer genetic information between cells in Salmonella.
They named the process transduction.
The discovery explained how different species of bacteria quickly gain resistance to the same antibiotic.
His work gave scientists an experimental model whose simplicity and rapid growth made it ideal for genetic research.

According to Stanford, the process Lederberg discovered, the transfer of genetic information between bacteria for which he won the Nobel Prize, became a standard way for researchers to transfer genetic information between bacteria in the lab.
According to Rockefeller, the description of transduction led to the development of gene therapy and contributed to the boom in biotechnology and genetic engineering in the 1970s.
In 1957 he helped found a Department of Medical Genetics at Wisconsin, one of the first of its kind in the country, and headed it.
Lederberg was 33 when he won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, for the discovery that bacteria can mate and exchange genes.
He shared the 1958 prize with Edward Tatum and George Beadle, and was one of the youngest laureates.
Lederberg received half of the prize.
Prize motivation: his discoveries concerning genetic recombination and the organization of the genetic material of bacteria.
According to Stanford Magazine, he accepted Stanford's offer in 1958, days before he learned about the Nobel Prize.
According to the Stanford website, in 1959 he arrived at the Stanford School of Medicine as chair of the genetics department.

stations.title: Beyond bacteria: Mars, computers and governments

paragraphs.text: He coined the term exobiology, the study of the possibility of life beyond Earth.
According to the Stanford website, he designed experiments to detect life on Mars, which led to the Viking lander.
According to the National Library of Medicine, with Edward Feigenbaum he developed DENDRAL, the first expert system for scientific use.
According to the Times, between 1966 and 1971 he wrote a weekly column in The Washington Post on science education, on the role of scientists in society and on controversial issues.
According to Rockefeller, he advised nine American administrations, and worked to advance international science and human rights.
In 1978 he moved to Rockefeller as the university's fifth president, and served until June 1990.
During his tenure, the University Fellows Program was established there in 1985.
According to Stanford Magazine, he was one of Time's men of the year in 1960, and he also received the National Medal of Science and the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
In 1989 he received the U.S. National Medal of Science.
In 2012 an impact crater 87 km in diameter on Mars was named after him.
According to David Hamburg, and according to Stanford's dean of medicine Philip Pizzo, Lederberg was one of the great scientists of the 20th century.
According to Donald Kennedy, when he arrived at Stanford he was already a hero, the most important founder of bacterial genetics.
Lederberg died on February 2, 2008, at NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital, at the age of 82.
Rockefeller University announced his death, giving pneumonia as the cause.
He is survived by his wife Marguerite, Anne and David Kirsch.
According to Rockefeller, he is also survived by two grandchildren.
In 1986, Lederberg supported the Soviet account, according to which the anthrax outbreak in Sverdlovsk resulted from transmission from animals to humans.
Later investigations confirmed that the outbreak was caused by a leak of anthrax aerosol from a nearby military facility.

disagreements.question: When was mating between bacteria discovered?

versions.says: Nobel Prize website: Lederberg and Tatum showed it in 1946
Rockefeller: the question of how bacteria gain virulence and resistance was resolved in 1947, by a 22-year-old graduate student
Encyclopedia.com: in 1952 he and a colleague documented that bacteria genes do not spread solely through cell division

disagreements.question: When did his parents emigrate, and from where?

versions.says: The New York Times: his mother, Esther Goldenbaum, emigrated two years earlier from what is now Israel
National Library of Medicine: his parents emigrated from Palestine the year before
Nobel Prize website: his parents had emigrated shortly before from Israel

disagreements.question: How many papers did Lederberg publish?

versions.says: National Library of Medicine: more than 300 scientific and policy-related articles

disagreements.question: Is David Kirsch his son or his stepson?

versions.says: Rockefeller: one of their children, alongside Anne Lederberg

disagreements.question: In what year did Lederberg receive his doctorate from Yale?

versions.says: His autobiography on the Nobel Prize website: in 1948
